issues.legal_issue: A claimant seeking a declaration of ownership over disputed property must establish the claimed title before obtaining a decree.
material_facts: The plaintiff sought a declaration of ownership over a one-third share of the property.
The defendants disputed the plaintiff’s ownership and the registered ownership stood in the defendants’ favour.
The plaintiff produced no document of title in her name, and the Supreme Court upheld the finding that she had not established her title.
issues.conclusion: The plaintiff had to prove her claimed ownership and, having failed to do so, was not entitled to the decree; the High Court’s decision on this issue was correct.
issues.legal_principle: Under Sections 101 and 102 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872, the initial burden of proving a claimed legal right rests on the party seeking relief and does not shift unless that party first makes out a case. The Court relied on Anil Rishi v. Gurbaksh Singh and the principle stated in R.V.E. Venkatachala Gounder v. Arulmigu Viswesaraswami & V.P. Temple, including the distinction between the burden of proof and the shifting onus of proof.

predicates.title_based_claim: The claimant sought relief on the basis that the claimant owned the disputed property or a share in it.
predicates.title_is_disputed: The opposing party disputed the claimant’s ownership of the property.
predicates.claimant_failed_to_establish_title: The claimant did not establish the claimed ownership on the evidence presented.

issues.definition: When a claimant seeks relief based on ownership, ownership is disputed, and the claimant fails to establish title, the claimant is not entitled to a title decree.

issues.legal_issue: A High Court may interfere with concurrent factual findings in a second appeal when those findings result from ignoring material evidence or pleadings, applying the law erroneously, or placing the burden of proof on the wrong party.
material_facts: The trial court and first appellate court found for the plaintiff after treating the pleadings as showing no denial of the claimed ownership.
The principal defendant had specifically denied the plaintiff’s ownership claim, and the plaintiff had not produced a title document.
The High Court found that the lower courts had overlooked material pleadings and evidence and had proceeded on erroneous factual assumptions.
The High Court framed substantial questions of law and set aside the concurrent findings; the Supreme Court upheld that exercise of jurisdiction.
issues.conclusion: The High Court properly exercised its jurisdiction in the second appeal to set aside the concurrent findings, and the Supreme Court found no reason to interfere with its judgment.
issues.legal_principle: Section 100 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, generally bars reappreciation of evidence in a second appeal absent a substantial question of law, but interference may be justified where the lower courts ignore material evidence, act on no evidence, draw legally erroneous inferences, or wrongly cast the burden of proof. The Court relied on Hira Lal v. Gajjan and Hero Vinoth (Minor) v. Seshammal.

rule.if: second_appeal and concurrent_findings and (material_pleadings_ignored or material_evidence_ignored or findings_based_on_erroneous_inferences or burden_wrongly_cast)

predicates.second_appeal: The proceeding is a second appeal from lower-court decisions.
predicates.concurrent_findings: The lower courts reached concurrent factual findings.
predicates.material_pleadings_ignored: The lower courts failed to account for pleadings material to the disputed issue.
predicates.material_evidence_ignored: The lower courts failed to account for material evidence or proceeded without evidence capable of supporting their findings.
predicates.findings_based_on_erroneous_inferences: The lower courts drew findings from proved facts by applying the law erroneously.
predicates.burden_wrongly_cast: The lower courts placed the burden of proof on the wrong party.

issues.definition: In a second appeal involving concurrent findings, the findings may be set aside when material pleadings or evidence were ignored, the inferences were legally erroneous, or the burden of proof was wrongly placed.

issues.legal_issue: A party’s claimed ownership cannot be treated as admitted where the party asserting ownership is met by a clear denial from the opposing party whose title is in issue.
material_facts: The plaintiff asserted that the property was jointly owned by ancestors and that she succeeded to a one-third share.
The defendant who claimed ownership through a court auction specifically denied the plaintiff’s ownership and possession claim.
The other defendant’s position did not amount to an independent basis for deciding the title dispute, yet the lower courts treated the pleadings as admitting the plaintiff’s claimed share.
The Supreme Court upheld the High Court’s conclusion that the lower courts had wrongly found an admission of the plaintiff’s ownership.
issues.conclusion: The lower courts erred in treating the pleadings as an admission of the plaintiff’s ownership because the defendant claiming title had specifically denied it.
issues.legal_principle: An admission must be clear and unambiguous, and pleadings must be read as a whole rather than by relying on an isolated statement. The Court relied on Jeevan Diesels & Electricals Ltd. v. Jasbir Singh Chadha (HUF) and Rachakonda Venkat Rao v. R. Satya Bai; it also applied the burden-of-proof principles in Sections 101 and 102 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872.

rule.if: civil_title_dispute and ownership_claimed and title_claimant_opponent_clearly_denied_claim and other_opponent_did_not_deny_claim

predicates.civil_title_dispute: The proceeding concerns competing claims of ownership over property.
predicates.ownership_claimed: One side asserted ownership of the disputed property or a share in it.
predicates.title_claimant_opponent_clearly_denied_c: The opposing party claiming title clearly denied the asserted ownership.
predicates.other_opponent_did_not_deny_claim: Another opposing party did not separately deny the ownership assertion.

issues.definition: In a property ownership dispute, a clear denial by the opposing title claimant prevents the claim from being treated as admitted merely because another opposing party did not deny it.
